subChunks.title: Client Consultation & Research Plan Writing

storyBeats.txt: Research begins before you open a single document, Theodora said. It begins with the client. Who are they? What do they actually need? What do they think they need? Those are sometimes different questions.

The consultation is where you establish the research question, the scope, the budget, and the realistic expectations. A client who expects you to find William the Conqueror in their family tree by Tuesday needs a gentle, honest conversation before you take their money.

The research plan is where you commit to paper what you will do, in what order, and why. It is both a contract with the client and a discipline for yourself. It keeps the research focused. It prevents scope creep. And when the research goes somewhere unexpected — as it will — it provides a documented baseline from which to recalibrate.

subChunks.hookHtml:
The difference between an amateur genealogist and a professional is not simply that the professional charges a fee. It is that the professional has developed systems for managing the client relationship, scoping the research, and delivering results in a form that is useful to the client and defensible to scrutiny. Client consultation and research planning are the foundation of those systems.

A well-conducted initial consultation establishes: what the client's goal is; what they already know; what constraints they are operating under (budget, time, geographic accessibility); and what a realistic outcome looks like. A well-written research plan translates that consultation into a systematic, documented strategy that guides the work and communicates the methodology to the client before a single archive is opened.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Initial Consultation

The initial consultation serves several functions simultaneously: information gathering (what does the client already know?); expectation setting (what is realistically achievable?); scope definition (what specific question will this project address?); and contract framing (what will the work cost, how long will it take, and what will be delivered?).

Key questions to ask: What is your primary research goal? What have you already researched? What records do you already hold? Are there family oral traditions that may or may not be accurate? What is your budget for this project? Do you have a timeline? Have you previously worked with other genealogists on this question?

The consultation should be conducted in writing as much as possible — or at minimum, followed up with a written summary — so that both parties have a clear record of what was discussed and agreed. Email or a client intake form serves this purpose.

Setting Realistic Expectations

Managing client expectations is one of the professional genealogist's most important skills. Common unrealistic expectations include: that all ancestors can be found; that research will be completed in a fixed time regardless of what records survive; that a 'DNA test will tell us everything'; and that a family's oral traditions will be confirmed rather than contradicted.

The professional response is honest, not brutal. Explain what records exist, what their coverage is, and what the probability of finding the relevant information is. If a client wants to trace to 1600 in a parish where the registers were destroyed, explain that reality and propose achievable alternatives. Do not take on projects you have reason to believe cannot be completed satisfactorily.

The Research Plan

A research plan is a written document that specifies: the research question (precisely stated); what the client has already provided (existing documents, family knowledge, DNA results); what records will be searched and in what order; why each record type is expected to address the question; what alternative strategies will be pursued if primary records do not yield results; the project budget and timeline; and deliverables (what the client will receive at the end).

The research plan is both a professional document and a client communication tool. It should be written in plain language that a non-genealogist can understand, while being technically precise enough to guide the research. Avoid genealogical jargon without explanation; use it where it is precise, but define it.

Research Plan Structure

  1. Project summary: Client name, project date, research question, known information.
  2. Previous research review: What has already been researched, by whom, and what it found. Prevents duplication and establishes the starting point.
  3. Record types to be searched: Listed in priority order with justification for each. Include estimated search time and cost.
  4. DNA strategy: If DNA testing is relevant, describe the platform, the matching strategy, and how DNA results will be integrated with documentary research.
  5. Contingency plan: What will be done if primary records are unavailable, destroyed, or yield no results.
  6. Deliverables and timeline: What the client will receive (interim reports, final report, pedigree chart), and when.
  7. Budget: Estimated fees (researcher time), estimated disbursements (archive access, certificate fees, postal charges), and the billing arrangement.

Scope of Work and Hourly vs. Fixed Fee

Genealogical projects are billed either hourly (the researcher's time is charged at an agreed rate, with progress reported at agreed milestones) or as fixed-fee projects (a defined deliverable for a fixed price). Hourly billing is more common in research work, since the amount of time required is genuinely uncertain. Fixed-fee billing is more common in report writing, indexing, or other tasks where the scope is well-defined.

All billing arrangements must be set out clearly in writing before work begins. The client must understand that genealogical research does not guarantee results — fees are for the researcher's time and expertise, not for a specific finding. This is a source of client dissatisfaction when not clearly communicated in advance.

Interim Reports

For longer projects, interim reports at agreed milestones are best practice. An interim report summarises: what has been searched; what was found; what has been ruled out; what the next steps are; and whether the project scope needs adjustment. Interim reports prevent the client from feeling left in the dark and allow scope adjustments before significant additional time is invested in a direction that no longer serves the client's needs.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a professional genealogist does in the first meeting with a new client, and why writing down a plan before starting the research is important.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A new client, Mrs. Davies, contacts you. She says: 'I want to find out if my family is connected to a famous Welsh poet of the 18th century with the same surname. My grandfather always said we were descendants, but we have no documentation. I have a budget of about £500 and I would like to know within six weeks.' Draft the key questions you would ask in the initial consultation and the first three items in a research plan for this project.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Initial consultation questions: What is the poet's full name and dates? What is Mrs. Davies's known earliest Welsh Davies ancestor — name, dates, location? Has any previous research been done on this connection? Does she hold any family documents (birth/marriage/death certificates, family bible, photographs, letters)? Has she or any family member done DNA testing? Is the £500 her total budget including disbursements (certificates, archive fees), or researcher fees only? Is the six-week timeline fixed, or an aspiration?

Setting expectations honestly: explaining that (a) a direct documented connection to an 18th-century individual through an undocumented claim is a challenging research goal; (b) the surname Davies is one of the most common in Wales, making surname matches unreliable; (c) £500 is a modest budget for this type of research — managing what is realistically achievable within that constraint is essential.

First three research plan items:

(1) Review existing documentation: Examine all certificates and documents Mrs. Davies holds for her known family. Identify the earliest documented Davies ancestor (name, dates, location). This is the baseline from which the research will begin and costs zero beyond researcher time.

(2) GRO and Welsh civil registration search: Trace Mrs. Davies's paternal Davies line back through civil registration (1837+) and then census returns, establishing the documented Welsh connection and the specific parish of origin. Budget: 3–4 hours researcher time + certificate fees.

(3) Parish register and Census search for known Welsh parish: Once the relevant Welsh parish is identified, search surviving parish registers and the 1841–1901 Welsh censuses for Davies family members in that parish. Cross-reference with known dates for the poet to identify any geographic overlap. At this stage we can assess whether a connection is plausible before committing further resources.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a complete research plan for the following scenario: Client is James Okafor, born in London in 1975 to a Nigerian father and English mother. His father died when he was 3 and he has no contact with his father's family. He wants to understand his Nigerian heritage and identify any living relatives. He has tested on AncestryDNA. His budget is £800. Write the research plan with all seven required sections.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Project Summary
Client: James Okafor. Date: [current date]. Question: Identify the family origins and living relatives of James's biological father, including geographic origin in Nigeria, family network, and possible contact with biological relatives.

2. Previous Research Review
Client has tested on AncestryDNA. No other prior research. Father's name known; no contact with father's family since age 3. No documents held relating to father except his name on James's birth certificate.

3. Records to be Searched
(a) James's birth certificate — will confirm father's full name, occupation, and address at time of birth. Essential first step; fee c.£12. (b) Electoral registers, 1975–1985 (GRO address tracing) — trace father's registered address to see if he remained in contact with any traceable address. (c) GRO death certificate search — confirm father's death date and cause; death certificate will name informant (possibly a relative). (d) Nigerian civil registration and church records — if father's state of origin can be identified from documents, research applicable records; FamilySearch has some Nigerian vital records. (e) AncestryDNA match analysis — apply Leeds Method clustering to the match list; African matches will be sparse but any close matches (above 200 cM) should be investigated with tree building.

4. DNA Strategy
Upload raw DNA to MyHeritage and FamilyTreeDNA to maximise Nigerian/African diaspora matches. Upload to GEDmatch for cross-platform matching. Y-DNA test (James is male) will determine patrilineal haplogroup — potentially identifying ethnic group of origin (Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, etc.). Search 23andMe's Ancestry Composition for Nigerian sub-regional breakdown.

5. Contingency Plan
If documentary records yield no Nigerian address or contact details, focus exclusively on DNA matching. If DNA matches are all distant (3rd cousin and further), the Mirror Tree method will be required. If no Nigerian matches appear at any tested platform, genetic genealogy has reached its current practical limit for this client's population; advise on specialist African DNA genealogy services.

6. Deliverables and Timeline
Week 1–2: documentary research (birth/death certificate, electoral register). Week 3–4: DNA analysis and tree building. Week 5–6: synthesis and report. Deliverable: written research report with all sources cited, pedigree chart for all documented connections, and annotated DNA match list.

7. Budget
Estimated researcher time: 8 hours @ £[rate]. Disbursements: certificates (c.£30), archive access (c.£20), DNA platform upload fees (free). Total estimated: £[calculation]. Billing: hourly with progress update at 4-hour milestone. Client to approve further work if scope adjustment is needed at milestone.
learningObjectives: Conduct an initial client consultation that establishes research question, existing knowledge, realistic expectations, scope, and budget.
Write a seven-section research plan that is both technically precise and accessible to a non-specialist client.
Set appropriate client expectations about research uncertainty, timelines, and the fee-for-time (not fee-for-result) model.
Describe the purpose and content of interim reports in longer genealogical projects.
commonMistakes: Accepting an ill-defined client request ('find my family') without establishing a precise research question — this leads to scope creep and client dissatisfaction.
Failing to document the agreed scope and budget in writing before starting work — verbal agreements are a source of disputes.
Implying or allowing a client to believe that fees are conditional on finding results rather than on researcher time and expertise.
Not including contingency plans in the research plan — clients should understand what happens if the primary records don't yield results.
assessmentCriteria: Research question is precisely and testably stated — not a vague aspiration.
Research plan includes all seven sections and is written in language accessible to a non-specialist.
Expectations about research uncertainty are addressed honestly and constructively.
Budget and billing arrangements are clearly specified, including the fee-for-time model.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The gradual expansion of a project beyond its originally agreed boundaries — a significant risk in genealogical research without a written plan and agreed scope.

A structured questionnaire completed by clients before the initial consultation, capturing existing knowledge, research goals, and relevant documents — reduces consultation time and ensures consistent information gathering.

Hourly billing charges for researcher time at an agreed rate (common in research work); fixed-fee billing sets a price for a defined deliverable. The distinction matters for setting client expectations about uncertain research outcomes.

A progress report delivered at agreed milestones during a longer project, summarising findings, ruling out dead ends, and proposing next steps — essential for client communication in extended research projects.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of a genealogical research plan?
options: To guarantee the client a specific research outcome
To document the research question, methodology, contingency strategies, deliverables, and budget before work begins
To list every archive that will be visited during the project
To prove the researcher's qualifications to the client
questions.correctAnswer: To document the research question, methodology, contingency strategies, deliverables, and budget before work begins
questions.explanationHtml: A research plan is a written agreement between researcher and client specifying what will be done, why, and at what cost. It focuses the research, manages expectations, and provides a documented baseline for any scope adjustments during the project.

questions.questionHtml: A client calls you after receiving your interim report and says: 'You've been working for 10 hours and haven't found anything yet. I expected results by now.' How should you respond?
options: Apologise and offer a refund for the hours worked

Explain that this is exactly why the research plan stated fees are for researcher time and expertise, not guaranteed results; review what has been ruled out; and discuss whether to continue or adjust scope
Promise to find the relevant record within the next 5 hours or work for free
End the project immediately and refund all fees
questions.correctAnswer: Explain that this is exactly why the research plan stated fees are for researcher time and expertise, not guaranteed results; review what has been ruled out; and discuss whether to continue or adjust scope
questions.explanationHtml: The research plan should have made clear that fees are for professional time and expertise, not guaranteed findings. The appropriate response is to refer to that agreed understanding, explain the value of the negative evidence gathered, and discuss how to proceed — continuing, adjusting scope, or concluding. A professional does not make promises they cannot keep.

questions.questionHtml: Why is it important to ask a new client whether they have previously worked with other genealogists on the same research question?
options: To check if you are in competition with another genealogist for the same client
To avoid duplicating research already completed, to assess the quality of any previous work, and to understand what conclusions were previously reached and why
Because previous genealogists may have a copyright claim over the client's family tree
APG ethics require all clients to disclose previous genealogists
questions.correctAnswer: To avoid duplicating research already completed, to assess the quality of any previous work, and to understand what conclusions were previously reached and why
questions.explanationHtml: Reviewing previous research avoids waste and allows the new researcher to build on (or critique, if methodologically flawed) prior work. It also reveals if the current project is partly motivated by disagreement with a previous researcher's conclusions — a dynamic that requires careful handling.
